notes: Gojoseon (traditionally 2333-108 BCE) has no reliable, verifiable list of rulers. Its only named ruler, Dangun, is a mythological/legendary founding figure recorded centuries after the fact (earliest surviving account: the 13th-century Samguk Yusa). No archaeological chronology of Gojoseon kings exists. Per brief instructions, Dangun is included below as a single traditional/mythological entry rather than inventing or padding a Gojoseon ruler list.

rulers.name: Dangun
rulers.summary: Legendary grandson of the god of heaven; traditional founder of Gojoseon, Korea's first kingdom, at Asadal.
rulers.contested: Mythological founding figure; no archaeological or contemporaneous evidence he existed, and the 2333 BCE date derives from a 15th-century CE reinterpretation of the 13th-century Samguk Yusa legend.
rulers.date_agreement: traditional: not an archaeological date; Britannica gives only the accession year (2333 BC) and no end date, so the -2240 end year here follows Wikipedia's traditional regnal-length convention, not an independently attested figure

rulers.name: Gwanggaeto the Great
rulers.summary: 19th king of Goguryeo; expanded the kingdom to its greatest territorial extent through rapid military conquest.
rulers.date_agreement: differs: Simple Wikipedia gives 393-413, while Britannica's Goguryeo/Sosurim articles and the Met Museum's rulers list give 391-413; the Samguk Sagi-derived 391 accession is the more commonly cited figure and is used here

rulers.name: Jangsu
rulers.summary: 20th king of Goguryeo; moved the capital to Pyongyang and presided over a 79-year reign, the longest in East Asian history.
rulers.date_agreement: differs: the Wikipedia infobox states 412-491 while the article's own prose and the Met Museum's rulers list both say 413-491; 413 (the year his father Gwanggaeto died) is used here as the majority figure

rulers.name: Seong of Baekje
rulers.summary: 26th king of Baekje; moved the capital to Sabi and revitalized the kingdom before dying in battle against Silla.
rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Jinheung of Silla
rulers.summary: 24th king of Silla; expanded Silla's territory greatly and organized the Hwarang warrior-scholar corps.
rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Muyeol of Silla
rulers.summary: 29th king of Silla, born Kim Chunchu; allied with Tang China and laid the groundwork for unifying the Three Kingdoms.
rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Munmu of Silla
rulers.summary: 30th king of Silla; completed the conquest of Goguryeo and Baekje, ending the Three Kingdoms period, before ruling on into Unified Silla.
rulers.date_agreement: matches: full reign is 661-681 (see Unified Silla entry below); this entry's end_year of 668 marks the fall of Goguryeo and close of the Three Kingdoms period per the brief's grouping, not the end of his reign

rulers.name: Munmu of Silla
rulers.summary: First ruler of Unified Silla; drove out Tang forces in 676 to gain sole control of most of the Korean peninsula.
rulers.date_agreement: matches: page gives his full reign as 661-681; 668 is used here as the start of the Unified Silla portion per this dataset's polity split, following Wikipedia's own statement that he 'is usually considered to have been the first ruler of the Unified Silla period'

rulers.name: Sinmun of Silla
rulers.summary: 31st king of Silla; centralized royal power and completed the administrative framework of the newly unified state.
rulers.date_agreement: differs: sources split between an end year of 691 and 692 (e.g. Wikipedia's infobox says 681-691 while its succession list and the Met Museum's rulers list say 681-692); 692 is used here as the majority figure

rulers.name: Gyeongdeok of Silla
rulers.summary: 35th king of Silla; presided over a cultural peak marked by Buddhist temple-building including Bulguksa.
rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Taejo Wang Geon
rulers.summary: Founder and first king of Goryeo; unified the Later Three Kingdoms in 936, ending the post-Silla division of Korea.
rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Gwangjong of Goryeo
rulers.summary: Fourth king of Goryeo; freed enslaved war prisoners, created the civil service examination system, and curbed noble power.
rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Seongjong of Goryeo
rulers.summary: Sixth king of Goryeo; institutionalized Confucian governance and a centralized bureaucratic administrative system.

source.citation: 'Taejo of Goryeo', Wikipedia (Goryeo monarch succession table)

rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Chungnyeol of Goryeo
rulers.summary: 25th king of Goryeo; first Goryeo king married to a Mongol Yuan princess, ruling as a Mongol-period vassal monarch.
rulers.date_agreement: matches: page shows two separate reigns (1274-1298 and 1298-1308) with a brief 1298 abdication in between; overall span 1274-1308 given here matches secondary sources such as Encyclopedia.com's succession list

rulers.name: Gongmin of Goryeo
rulers.summary: 31st king of Goryeo; broke free of Mongol Yuan overlordship and reasserted Korean sovereignty late in the dynasty.
rulers.date_agreement: matches: Britannica gives 1352-74 for the start of major reforms under his reign; the reign span 1351-1374 itself follows the Goryeo succession table on Wikipedia's Taejo of Goryeo page

rulers.name: Taejo of Joseon
rulers.summary: Founder and first king of Joseon; overthrew Goryeo and established the dynasty that would rule Korea until 1910.
rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Sejong the Great
rulers.summary: Fourth king of Joseon; created Hangul and oversaw Korea's greatest era of scientific and cultural achievement.
rulers.date_agreement: differs: Britannica gives 1419-50 (using the lunar new-year convention for his accession), while Wikipedia and the Sejong Pyeongchang center give the Gregorian accession date of 18 September 1418; 1418 is used here as the enthronement year

rulers.name: Seongjong of Joseon
rulers.summary: Ninth king of Joseon; compiled the Gyeongguk daejeon legal code, completing Joseon's institutional foundations.
rulers.date_agreement: differs: Wikipedia's precise Gregorian reign dates (9 January 1470 - 29 January 1495) place his accession/death a few weeks into the following calendar year versus the conventional lunar-calendar years 1469-1494 used by most secondary sources (e.g. New World Encyclopedia, kiddle); 1469-1494 is used here as the conventional figure

rulers.name: Yeonsangun
rulers.summary: Tenth ruler of Joseon; deposed in a coup after a tyrannical reign marked by purges of scholar-officials.
rulers.date_agreement: differs: Wikipedia's precise reign dates (29 January 1495 - 28 September 1506) again reflect the Gregorian-vs-lunar year offset; the conventional lunar-year figures 1494-1506 are used here to match Seongjong's end year and most secondary sources

rulers.name: Seonjo of Joseon
rulers.summary: 14th king of Joseon; his reign was defined by the Imjin War, Japan's devastating 1592-98 invasions of Korea.
rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Yeongjo of Joseon
rulers.summary: 21st king of Joseon; his 52-year reign, the dynasty's longest, brought reform and recovery after earlier wars.
rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Jeongjo of Joseon
rulers.summary: 22nd king of Joseon; patronized scholarship and reform, building the Hwaseong Fortress as a symbol of royal renewal.
rulers.date_agreement: matches

rulers.name: Gojong
rulers.summary: 26th and last king of Joseon; later proclaimed Korea's first emperor before Japanese pressure forced his abdication.
rulers.date_agreement: differs: sources split between 1863 and 1864 for his accession (Wikipedia's Joseon overview article says 'In 1863, King Gojong took the throne', while his own biography page gives the precise Gregorian date 16 January 1864, corresponding to a lunar-calendar 1863 date); Britannica's biography gives no explicit reign dates at all. 1864 (the Gregorian coronation year) and 1897 (when he proclaimed the Korean Empire, ending the Joseon-kingdom phase of his rule per this dataset's polity scope) are used here.
